fields.Front: What does Unit 2 cover, and which internally driven processes does it deliberately exclude and why?
fields.Back: Unit 2 is confined to INTERNAL energy release: earthquakes, volcanic eruptions and their side effects. It excludes landslides, land subsidence and similar processes - they are too small ever to make it onto the catastrophic events scale.

fields.Front: List Earth's layers by CHEMICAL composition (older terminology), centre outward.
fields.Back:
Inner core: hot, SOLID nearly pure metal (iron and nickel).
Outer core: similarly hot but LIQUID metal (molten iron and nickel).
Mantle: a very large volume of dense silicate and oxide minerals.
Crust: a thin outer shell, oceanic or continental.
Topped off by oceans and atmosphere.

fields.Front: Define the asthenosphere, and why does it behave differently from the mesosphere?
fields.Back: A thin zone of the upper mantle with the SAME composition as the mesosphere, but because it lies nearer the top of the mantle it is under much less confining pressure, so it behaves like a hot plastic ('soft plastic') and may locally even be fluid.
The crust PLUS the really thin, essentially cold and brittle top layer of the mantle that is 'stuck' to the crust - Earth's rigid outer shell.

fields.Front: Approximate depths to the base of each layer (Fig. 2).
fields.Back: Lithosphere about 100 km; asthenosphere about 350 km; mesosphere (base of mantle) 2,890 km; outer core 5,150 km; centre of Earth 6,371 km.
Ocean water 1.03; continental crust 2.7; upper mantle 3.3 then 3.6; mesosphere 4.3 rising to 5.7 at its base; outer core 9.7 to 11.8; inner core 14 to 16.

Accretion: growth of a body by collision and sticking of smaller objects - how Earth got its mass, starting from cold material.
Differentiation: gravity sorting an already-molten planet by density, heavy material to the core, light material outward - how Earth got its layers. Do not swap them.

fields.Front: What are the two types of crust, and what defines 'plates' and 'tectonics'?
fields.Back: Crust types: oceanic and continental. Plates: large segments of Earth's crust/lithosphere. Tectonics: the processes by which plates interact along their boundaries in response to heat energy escaping from inside Earth.

fields.Front: How are the edges of tectonic plates defined?
fields.Back: By the traces (lines) of earthquakes and volcanoes, which fall in very clear lines around Earth and are concentrated along subduction zones (convergent boundaries) and transform faults.

fields.Front: Why did earthquakes and volcanic eruptions stop being considered random events?
fields.Back: More than 100 years ago it was slowly realized that most (but certainly not all) earthquakes and eruptions are associated with the edges of large segments of Earth's crust, later called plates; even more slowly it emerged that those plates interact along the boundaries in response to escaping internal heat.

fields.Front: What does the rest of Unit 2 cover, chapter by chapter?
fields.Back:
Ch 3: plate tectonics (Wegener's drift plus heat-driven mechanisms).
Ch 4: earthquakes at the different plate boundaries.
Ch 5: the very largest earthquakes and the tsunami from them.
Ch 6: earthquakes that seldom make catastrophes but shake populated regions.
Ch 7: volcanic eruption basics, plate boundaries and mantle plumes.
Ch 8: subduction-zone volcanoes and giant resurgent calderas.
Ch 9: flood basalt, possibly linked to mass extinctions.

fields.Text: Earth's layers by PHYSICAL properties, surface to centre: {{c1::lithosphere}}, {{c1::asthenosphere}}, {{c1::mesosphere}}, {{c1::outer core}}, {{c1::inner core}} - the mantle being split into mesosphere, asthenosphere and the brittle top of the lithosphere.
The {{c1::mesosphere}} is the lower, thick zone of the old mantle: very dense rock that behaves as a {{c1::solid}} (Fig. 2 labels it '{{c1::stiff plastic}}').

The lithosphere = the {{c1::crust}} plus the cold, brittle uppermost {{c1::mantle}}; the same mantle {{c1::composition}} behaves differently at different temperature and pressure, which is why the physical terminology is more useful.

{{c1::Differentiation}} is the process, once Earth was hot and liquid enough for material to move freely, of {{c1::heavy}} material moving by gravity to the core and {{c1::lighter}} material moving outward - producing the layered structure.
{{c1::Accretion}} is the growth of a body as smaller objects (asteroids, meteoroids, dust) {{c1::stick to it}}; Earth's growth began with accretion of {{c1::cold}} material.

EXAM TRAP: the Unit 2 Introduction gives Earth's interior as {{c1::7200-7500}} degrees C, while Chapter 3 gives the inner core as {{c1::5000-7000}} degrees C ('about as hot as the surface of the Sun') - quote whichever {{c1::chapter}} the question comes from.

EXAM TRAP: the lithosphere is {{c1::not}} the same as the crust (it is crust + cold brittle uppermost mantle), and the asthenosphere is {{c1::not}} a molten layer - it is a hot {{c1::plastic}} that is only {{c1::locally}} fluid.
